paras: The threatened lynching of James Little took place in Greene County, New York, on July 14 and 15, 1903, when crowds of farmers, striking moulders and river men sought to lynch Little, a 19-year-old Black man accused of criminally assaulting 11-year-old Emma Cole near New Baltimore. Deputies moved him from the Coxsackie lockup to the Catskill jail before the crowd acted, and the next day disarmed the girl's father, who drew a revolver when Little was brought back for arraignment. Wire dispatches carried the case nationally, and Southern papers cited it as a Northern instance of the "usual crime" and the mob.

The Sun described Little as a slightly built 19-year-old who had left a travelling circus at Albany and was walking home to New Jersey. Moulders at Coxsackie were on strike, and July 14 was the strikers' "benefit day," crowding the town.

On the morning of July 14 Emma Cole, a farmer's daughter, was picking berries near New Baltimore with her younger sister and Maud Lobdell when Little asked the girls for food. According to the Sun and the Tribune, he dragged Emma into the woods, threw aside the Lobdell girl and threatened the child with death before fleeing; the papers stated as fact that he had "criminally assaulted" her. Roy Cutler caught him on the railroad track near Coxsackie, and he was put in the lockup there, where the papers said he confessed.

Farmers headed by Emma's father, Joseph Cole, then set out for Coxsackie, joined in the wire account by striking moulders and river men "all frankly vowing their intention to lynch the negro." The Sun said about one hundred men visited the flimsy lockup and withdrew to a hotel to discuss hanging Little from a telegraph pole. Meanwhile Deputy Sheriff Sumner Van Loon took him by the steamer Ursula to the Catskill jail, and Cole told the Sun, "If my plans carry, Little will not get out of here alive."

On July 15 Little was returned by boat to New Baltimore under "an especially strong sheriff's posse." A crowd of farmers, striking moulders and boat hands met the boat, and Cole drew a revolver as it docked before Deputy Sheriff Gould disarmed and calmed him. The justice of the peace delayed the arraignment two hours until a lawyer arrived from Catskill, and by then, with the child reported improving, the Worcester Spy said danger of an outbreak had subsided.

Little pleaded not guilty, waived examination and was bound over to the Greene County grand jury, then returned to the Catskill jail in default of bail. No arrest of anyone in the crowds appears in the coverage. On November 12 he pleaded guilty at Catskill and was sentenced to twenty years in Clinton Prison.

The story ran mainly as two Associated Press dispatches from Albany, printed from Texas to Montana, while the Sun and the Tribune sent their own accounts. Headlines credited the officers, as in the Courier-Journal's "QUICK WIT Of Deputy Saves Neck of a Negro," or the spread of mob feeling, as in the Guthrie Daily Leader's "Negro Lynching Fever Reaches New York." White papers reported the assault and confession as fact; the Washington Evening Star wrote of the "Little Victim in Desperate Condition From Treatment of the Brute."

Southern editorials used the case as a Northern parallel: Richmond's Times Dispatch called it "Another case of the 'usual crime'," and the Columbia Herald, quoting the Courier-Journal, said such assaults and mobs were "more frequent just now in the North than in the South." An Arizona Republican editorial on lynching noted that sheriffs had protected the accused.

The two Black weeklies in the coverage carried only wire copy without comment. The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran the arraignment dispatch as "Father Tries to Shoot," and the Cleveland Gazette the first dispatch as "LYNCHERS FOILED," with a subhead calling Little "Guilty of a Brutal Assault."

The Coxsackie crowd numbered 150 farmers in the wire, about one hundred in the Sun and 1,500 in the Cleveland Gazette's printing of the wire, likely a misprint. Little's home was given as Somerville or Summerhurst, New Jersey, and the justice as Joseph Nelson, Joel Nelson or Joel Nason.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of James Little
bases: Crowds of farmers, strikers and river men set out to lynch the jailed Little at Coxsackie on July 14 and gathered again at New Baltimore on July 15, where the girl's father drew a revolver; officers kept him from them (A1, A5, A10).

A crowd of about 100 to 150 vowed to lynch Little for the alleged assault and discussed hanging him, but a deputy removed him and he was later tried and sentenced, so no one was killed (A1, A5, A47); it is a threatened lynching.

The Sun and the Tribune sent separate Albany accounts that agree with the Associated Press wire on the assault charge, the Coxsackie crowd and the removal to Catskill, and several reports confirm the July 15 revolver incident (A1, A2, A5, A10, A25).

accounts.gist: Returned to New Baltimore under a strong posse, Little faced a crowd of farmers, moulders and boat hands; Joseph Cole drew a revolver and was disarmed by Deputy Gould; Little was bound over.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP text, headlined on the deputy's 'QUICK WIT' or the mob ('MOB THREATENS A PRISONER'), stating the assault and confession as fact.
New York papers ran their own accounts ('NEAR A LYNCHING UP-STATE', 'NEW-YORK MOB MENACES NEGRO') crediting officers with averting a lynching.
Southern papers called it the 'usual crime' by a 'negro brute' and used it to argue that mobs were now as common in the North.
The Arizona Republican, in an editorial quoting Justice Brewer that lynchers are murderers, listed the case and noted the sheriffs protected the accused, while doubting public opinion would change.
The Cleveland Gazette ran the wire under 'LYNCHERS FOILED' and the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate under 'Father Tries to Shoot', with no comment.
